Differential abundance: limma's moderated t, contrasts, and the tests around it

Source: vignettes/stats.Rmd
stats.Rmd

Most proteomics differential-abundance analyses end in limma: a linear model per protein, with each protein’s noisy variance shrunk toward what all the proteins together say (empirical-Bayes moderation, Smyth 2004). R has limma. These functions are the same method computed by mzLib, so an analysis in R reports the statistics MetaMorpheus and the Python and Rust bindings report, from the same code. The first section lets you check the agreement rather than take it on trust.

question function mzLib method
which features change with a coefficient, and how surely? stats_fit() LinearModel.Fit, EmpiricalBayes.Moderate (#1341) limma lmFit + eBayes(legacy = TRUE)
which of my p-values survive a false discovery rate? stats_adjust() MultipleTesting.BenjaminiHochberg Benjamini and Hochberg 1995
what is one feature’s effect, pooled across studies? stats_meta() RandomEffectsMeta.Pool (#1357) DerSimonian and Laird 1986, as metafor rma(method = "DL")
which features differ by a contrast, within what interval? stats_fit(contrasts = ) EmpiricalBayes.ModerateContrasts (#1452) limma contrasts.fit + topTable(confint = )
what do several studies’ p-values say together? stats_combine_p() PValueCombination.Fisher, .Stouffer (#1367) Fisher 1925, Stouffer 1949
which features rise or fall with a per-sample trait? stats_correlate() SpearmanCorrelation.Correlate, .PartialCorrelate (#1367, #1446) R cor.test(method = "spearman"), ppcor pcor.test
does a 0/1 outcome (detected or not) follow a coefficient? stats_fit_logistic() LogisticRegression.Fit (#1367) R glm(family = binomial) per feature
which features change, when samples come in groups? stats_fit_mixed() MixedModel.Fit (#1367) nlme::lme() with a random intercept per group
the same, when some samples are only counted (k of n trials)? stats_fit_latent_mixed() LogitNormalMixedModel.Fit (#1469) lme4::glmer() and lmer() in one model
how does a count’s chance of success follow the latent value? stats_fit_link() LogitNormalMixedModel.FitLink (#1469) maximum likelihood over the cells
does a search really control its FDR? stats_entrapment_fdp() EntrapmentFdp.Sweep (#1385) Wen et al. 2025, as FDRBench

stats_fit() already adjusts its own p-values, so you need stats_adjust() only for p-values from somewhere else, and stats_meta() only when you have one estimate per study.

Check it against limma

mzLib’s test suite carries a frozen limma run: 400 features, 12 samples with missing values, a design of intercept, age in decades and sex, and limma’s eBayes output for the age coefficient. This package ships the input and limma’s output in extdata/stats/:

data <- system.file("extdata", "stats", package = "mzLibR")
fit <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                 file.path(data, "limma_reference_design.tsv"), "age_decades")
fit
#> <mzlibr_moderated_fit> 400 features x 12 samples, testing age_decades
#>   fitted 400, too_few_observations 0, rank_deficient 0
#>   prior df 4.532 (moments_legacy)
#>   ! residual df differ between features: these are eBayes(legacy = TRUE) statistics
fit$coefficient_names
#> [1] "Intercept"   "age_decades" "sex"

Compare every feature with what limma said:

limma <- read.delim(file.path(data, "limma_ebayes_notrend.tsv"))
worst <- function(ours, theirs) max(abs(ours - theirs) / abs(theirs))
c(t = worst(fit$records$t, limma$t_age),
  p_value = worst(fit$records$p_value, limma$p_age),
  bh_adjusted = worst(fit$records$bh_adjusted, limma$bh_age),
  posterior_variance = worst(fit$records$posterior_variance, limma$s2_post),
  df_total = worst(fit$records$df_total, limma$df_total))
#>                  t            p_value        bh_adjusted posterior_variance 
#>       1.612212e-11       2.414497e-13       2.414120e-13       3.156851e-14 
#>           df_total 
#>       3.727223e-16

Every relative difference is below 1e-8. With limma installed you can run it yourself on the same input, limma::eBayes(limma::lmFit(y, x), legacy = TRUE); this package’s tests do exactly that, and bh_adjusted is p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH").

Which limma: the legacy estimator. This matches eBayes(legacy = TRUE). When features have different residual degrees of freedom, limma 3.61 and later default to a different prior estimator. Omitting missing values per feature is exactly what makes residual df differ, so on most label-free data default limma reports a slightly different prior and different moderated statistics. The fit says when your input is such a case:

fit$residual_df_differ
#> [1] TRUE

A real experiment with a known answer

mzLib’s RNA test data (mzLib #1388) holds a dilution series - real mass-spectrometry data where the right answer is known in advance. Across 27 runs the lncRNA MALAT1 was loaded at 500, 250 or 125 ng, while the luciferase transcript FLuc stayed at 500 ng. Halving MALAT1 should read as a log2 fold change of -1, quartering it as -2.

The responses are each oligo’s log2 FlashLFQ intensity minus that run’s median log2 intensity of the FLuc-only oligos (blank where FlashLFQ detected nothing), one row per oligo named <transcript>:<sequence>. The design has an intercept, so each coefficient is the change from the 500 ng runs:

design <- read.delim(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"))
table(malat_250ng = design$malat_250ng, malat_125ng = design$malat_125ng)
#>            malat_125ng
#> malat_250ng  0  1
#>           0  7  8
#>           1 12  0
fit <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                 file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
fit$status_counts
#>               fitted too_few_observations       rank_deficient 
#>                  212                  214                   66

Most oligos could not be fitted, and the fit says why rather than dropping them. An oligo seen in two or three runs has no residual variance to estimate (too_few_observations); one seen only in the 500 ng runs cannot have a 250 ng effect (rank_deficient). Both are rows with NA statistics, and neither enters the Benjamini-Hochberg family.

The question the experiment was designed to answer, as the median log2 fold change per transcript:

fitted <- fit$records[fit$records$status == "fitted", ]
fitted$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", fitted$feature)
keep <- fitted$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc")
aggregate(estimate ~ transcript + coefficient, data = fitted[keep, ], FUN = median)
#>   transcript coefficient   estimate
#> 1       FLuc malat_125ng -0.0458699
#> 2     MALAT1 malat_125ng -1.0144266
#> 3       FLuc malat_250ng -0.2164214
#> 4     MALAT1 malat_250ng -0.8914901

Half the MALAT1 reads as about -0.9 against a known -1; a quarter reads as about -1 against a known -2. The second is compressed by about half. The statistics did not create that: the estimates are ordinary least squares, and moderation changes only their standard errors. FLuc sits near 0 largely by construction, since every run was normalised to it.

Which oligos pass a 5% false discovery rate?

hits <- fitted[!is.na(fitted$bh_adjusted) & fitted$bh_adjusted < 0.05, ]
table(hits$coefficient, hits$transcript)
#>              
#>               20mer2 FLuc MALAT1
#>   malat_125ng      2    0      4
#>   malat_250ng      0    1      2

Few, and not all of them true. Two of the quarter-load calls are 20-mer oligos, loaded at a constant amount. A 5% false discovery rate bounds the expected share of wrong calls; it does not promise none, and a known-answer experiment is how you see it happen.

Unequal degrees of freedom: the marginal-likelihood prior

This experiment is the case the note on limma’s legacy estimator warns about: oligos are missing from different runs, so they have different residual degrees of freedom, and the default prior is limma’s legacy estimator:

c(residual_df_differ = fit$residual_df_differ, estimator = fit$prior$estimator,
  prior_df = round(fit$prior$df, 1))
#> residual_df_differ          estimator           prior_df 
#>             "TRUE"   "moments_legacy"             "19.6"

mzLib has a second estimator for exactly this case, "marginal_likelihood" (mzLib #1368). It fits the prior by maximum likelihood with each oligo’s own degrees of freedom, so an oligo seen in five runs counts as five runs’ worth of evidence about the variance, not as an average one. Ask for it by name:

ml <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"),
                estimator = "marginal_likelihood")
c(estimator = ml$prior$estimator, prior_df = round(ml$prior$df, 1))
#>             estimator              prior_df 
#> "marginal_likelihood"                  "11"
ml_fitted <- ml$records[ml$records$status == "fitted", ]
ml_hits <- ml_fitted[!is.na(ml_fitted$bh_adjusted) & ml_fitted$bh_adjusted < 0.05, ]
table(ml_hits$coefficient, sub(":.*$", "", ml_hits$feature))
#>              
#>               20mer2 MALAT1
#>   malat_125ng      2      4
#>   malat_250ng      0      1

The prior df falls: once each oligo’s own degrees of freedom count, the data support less shrinkage toward the common variance. The estimates are the same least-squares numbers; only the standard errors move, and with them the calls - compare this table with the one above. At half load the FLuc call is gone, which is right, since FLuc did not change.

  • It is mzLib’s own estimator, not limma’s. Default limma (3.61 and later) handles unequal degrees of freedom with a different method (fitFDistUnequalDF1), so expect small differences from default limma.
  • mzLib keeps "moments_legacy" the default, so that stats_fit() reproduces eBayes(legacy = TRUE) exactly. Leaving estimator out always means mzLib’s default, and prior$estimator says which one you got.
  • A prior df of about 0.05 is a floor, not a finding. mzLib searches d0 from e^-3 upward.
  • One prior serves the whole call: every coefficient and every contrast is moderated with it.

Contrasts: any comparison, with a confidence interval

A design’s coefficients answer one kind of question: each level against the baseline. The questions a scientist asks are often other comparisons: 500 ng against 250 ng when the baseline is 125 ng, or the mean of two groups against a third. Each is a contrast, a weighted sum of the coefficients, and stats_fit(contrasts = ) tests it with the same moderated t, plus a confidence interval: limma’s contrasts.fit(), eBayes() and topTable(confint = 0.95).

You rarely write the weights yourself. diff_design() builds the design from your sample sheet and writes the contrasts beside it. With no reference level, every pair of levels is a contrast:

samples <- system.file("extdata", "diff", "malat_dilution_samples.tsv", package = "mzLibR")
design <- diff_design(samples, factors = list(factor_spec("malat_load")),
                      out = file.path(tempdir(), "malat_pairs"))
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
#> [1] "intercept"        "malat_load=250ng" "malat_load=500ng"
stratum$warnings
#> [1] "No reference level was declared for factor 'malat_load', so every pair of its levels is compared (GR-14). Levels: 125ng, 250ng, 500ng."
labels <- setNames(design$records$label, design$records$contrast_id)
labels
#>                                     c1                                     c2 
#> "malat_load=250ng vs malat_load=125ng" "malat_load=500ng vs malat_load=125ng" 
#>                                     c3 
#> "malat_load=500ng vs malat_load=250ng"

mzLib took the first level, 125 ng, as the coding baseline, and wrote design_1.tsv and contrasts_1.tsv. Fit the design and test every contrast in the file. No coefficient is named, so the coefficient table is empty and every answer is in contrasts:

pairs <- stats_fit(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"), stratum$design_file,
                   contrasts = stratum$contrasts_file)
pairs$contrasts
#> <mzlibr_moderated_contrasts> 3 contrast(s) x 492 features, 95% intervals
#>   c1: 0 1 0
#>   c2: 0 0 1
#>   c3:  0 -1  1
c(coefficient_rows = pairs$row_count, contrast_rows = pairs$contrasts$row_count)
#> coefficient_rows    contrast_rows 
#>                0             1476

The weights are on pairs$coefficient_names. c1 and c2 are single coefficients. c3 is not: it is the 500 ng coefficient minus the 250 ng one, a comparison no column of this design holds. The answers are known in advance, +1, +2 and +1 in log2, so look at the MALAT1 oligos:

known <- c(c1 = 1, c2 = 2, c3 = 1)
summary_of <- function(id) {
  r <- pairs$contrasts$records
  r <- r[r$contrast == id & r$status == "fitted" & startsWith(r$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
  c(known = known[[id]], median = round(median(r$estimate), 2), oligos = nrow(r),
    interval_holds_it = sum(r$confidence_low <= known[[id]] & known[[id]] <= r$confidence_high),
    excludes_zero = sum(!(r$confidence_low <= 0 & 0 <= r$confidence_high)))
}
t(sapply(c("c1", "c2", "c3"), summary_of))
#>    known median oligos interval_holds_it excludes_zero
#> c1     1   0.18    116               103             7
#> c2     2   1.01    116               105            23
#> c3     1   0.89    116               109            16
  • Each oligo’s 95% interval is wide. It holds the known change for most oligos, and also holds 0 for most of them: one oligo, measured in a handful of runs, cannot tell a doubling from no change. The medians across oligos are much more precise than any one interval.
  • The contrasts locate the compression seen above. 500 ng against 250 ng reads close to its known +1; 250 ng against 125 ng reads far less. The shortfall is between the two lower loads.
  • The intervals are per feature and not adjusted. For a decision across features use bh_adjusted, which each contrast has over its own fitted features.

Each row of pairs$contrasts$records carries what a coefficient row does, plus confidence_low and confidence_high, in response units per contrast unit: a log2 fold change here.

Your own contrasts. A contrasts file is a header of a contrast id column and then exactly the design’s coefficient columns, in any order, then one row per contrast: its id and one weight per coefficient. To compare the mean of 250 ng and 125 ng against 500 ng on the design above:

contrast           intercept  malat_load=250ng  malat_load=500ng
low_mean_vs_500    0          0.5               -1

(125 ng is the baseline, so its coefficient is 0 and needs no weight of its own.) A column the design lacks, a design column the file lacks, a weight that is not a number, or a row of all zeros is refused.

The traps:

  • A stratum can skip a contrast id. Ids are numbered once over the whole analysis, so c1 is the same comparison in every stratum, but a stratum without samples on both sides lists it in not_run instead. Read the labels from diff_design(), as above.
  • With missing values the standard error is exact per feature, computed on the samples that feature was observed in. limma’s contrasts.fit() approximates it there, so on data with missing values these numbers differ from limma’s by design; with complete data they agree.
  • A contrast of one coefficient is that coefficient’s test, number for number. Asking for both in one call costs nothing: the model is fitted once and the prior is shared.
  • confidence = 0.9 (a fraction) changes the level; leave it out for mzLib’s default, and contrasts$confidence_level reports the level used.
  • It needs the pyMzLib 0.6.0 bridge. An older bridge ignores --contrasts and --estimator, so stats_fit() stops with an error naming the bridge it needs rather than return a fit that did not do what you asked.

Your own data

stats_fit() reads two tab-separated files: a responses table, one row per feature and one column per sample, and a design, one row per sample, matched to the responses’ columns by name. write.table(x, path, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE) writes either. Three things decide whether the answer means what you think:

  • Log-transform first. The model is additive in whatever you pass; with log2 intensities, estimate is a log2 fold change.
  • A 0 is an observation. Many quantification tables write 0 for “not measured”. Make those cells NA, or they are fitted as a real zero; zero_count counts them and a caveat says so.
  • The design is used as written. Include the intercept column yourself. diff_design() writes one from a sample sheet, with a contrasts file for any comparison that is no single column; see vignette("diff", package = "mzLibR").

P-values from anywhere 

adjusted <- stats_adjust(c(0.0002, 0.004, 0.019, NA, 0.031, 0.2, NaN, 0.74))
adjusted$tested_count
#> [1] 6
adjusted$records
#>   p_value bh_adjusted
#> 1  0.0002      0.0012
#> 2  0.0040      0.0120
#> 3  0.0190      0.0380
#> 4      NA          NA
#> 5  0.0310      0.0465
#> 6  0.2000      0.2400
#> 7      NA          NA
#> 8  0.7400      0.7400

NA marks a feature that was not tested: it stays NA and is not counted in m. Do not write 1 for it; that enlarges the family.

Pooling across studies

stats_meta() takes one row per study - feature, estimate, standard_error - and pools each feature with the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. These are metafor’s own reference cases, from mzLib’s test data:

inputs <- read.delim(file.path(data, "metafor_dl_inputs.tsv"))
pooled <- stats_meta(data.frame(feature = inputs$case, estimate = inputs$yi,
                                standard_error = inputs$sei))
pooled$records[, c("feature", "studies", "estimate", "tau2", "i_squared", "direction_agree",
                   "direction_disagree", "leave_one_out_max_delta")]
#>         feature studies   estimate       tau2 i_squared direction_agree
#> 1   homogeneous       5  0.3096950 0.00000000 0.0000000               5
#> 2 heterogeneous       6  0.2512721 0.07516970 0.8227530               5
#> 3   two_studies       2 -0.2000000 0.06000000 0.4800000               1
#> 4  random_eight       8  0.1069573 0.09113603 0.8123322               6
#>   direction_disagree leave_one_out_max_delta
#> 1                  0              0.01413259
#> 2                  1              0.09481756
#> 3                  1              0.30000000
#> 4                  2              0.07461657
metafor <- read.delim(file.path(data, "metafor_dl_results.tsv"))
worst(pooled$records$estimate[match(metafor$case, pooled$records$feature)], metafor$estimate)
#> [1] 3.892522e-16

direction_agree and leave_one_out_max_delta are the two checks a reader of a pooled result asks for first: how many studies point the same way, and how far the answer moves without any one of them. The interval uses a normal reference and does not widen for few studies, so treat a pooled estimate from two or three studies with care.

Combining p-values across studies

Sometimes all you have from each study is a p-value. stats_combine_p() turns several independent p-values for the same feature into one, by one of two rules: "fisher", X = -2 sum ln p against chi-square on 2k degrees of freedom, driven by the smallest p-values; or "stouffer", Z = sum w z / sqrt(sum w^2) against the standard normal, which weighs every study (for example by the square root of its sample size). There is no default: mzLib prefers neither, so you choose. mzLib’s own reference cases show the difference:

cases <- read.delim(file.path(data, "combination_inputs.tsv"))
cases[cases$case == "mixed", ]
#>     case     p weight
#> 21 mixed 0.001    1.5
#> 22 mixed 0.999    2.5
#> 23 mixed 0.500    3.5
#> 24 mixed 0.050    4.5
#> 25 mixed 0.950    5.5
fisher <- stats_combine_p(data.frame(feature = cases$case, p_value = cases$p), method = "fisher")
stouffer <- stats_combine_p(data.frame(feature = cases$case, p_value = cases$p, weight = cases$weight),
                            method = "stouffer")
data.frame(feature = fisher$records$feature, studies = fisher$records$studies,
           fisher = signif(fisher$records$p_value, 3), weighted_stouffer = signif(stouffer$records$p_value, 3))
#>   feature studies   fisher weighted_stouffer
#> 1     few       3 8.71e-02          0.150000
#> 2    tiny       4 3.14e-11          0.002280
#> 3     one       1 3.70e-02          0.037000
#> 4    many      12 1.13e-01          0.032300
#> 5   mixed       5 1.91e-02          0.713000
#> 6    tail       3 2.14e-18          0.000836

In mixed, one p-value of 0.001 sits among four that disagree. Fisher says the five studies together are significant, because one of them is; weighted Stouffer says they are not, because the heaviest study points the other way. Both agree with R’s pchisq() and qnorm():

r_answers <- read.delim(file.path(data, "combination_results.tsv"))
c(fisher = worst(fisher$records$p_value, r_answers$fisher_p),
  weighted_stouffer = worst(stouffer$records$p_value, r_answers$weighted_p))
#>            fisher weighted_stouffer 
#>      5.083515e-15      3.632781e-15

The trap: two-sided p-values have no direction. Both rules combine one-sided p-values. A two-sided p-value - which is what stats_fit() reports - says how surprising an effect is, not which way it went, so two studies that disagree count as two that agree. Here are three proteins, each tested in three cohorts (illustrative numbers, written here, not measured):

cohorts <- data.frame(
  feature = rep(c("up_everywhere", "flips_sign", "no_effect"), each = 3),
  p_value = c(0.003, 0.02, 0.3, 0.001, 0.004, 0.4, 0.6, 0.45, 0.85),
  weight = c(4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 3),
  effect = c(0.8, 0.5, 0.3, 1.2, -0.9, 0.2, -0.1, 0.1, -0.05))
ignored <- stats_combine_p(cohorts[, c("feature", "p_value", "weight")], method = "stouffer")
signed <- stats_combine_p(cohorts, method = "stouffer")
data.frame(feature = signed$records$feature, direction_ignored = signif(ignored$records$p_value, 2),
           signed = signif(signed$records$p_value, 2))
#>         feature direction_ignored  signed
#> 1 up_everywhere           6.2e-04 8.4e-05
#> 2    flips_sign           9.5e-05 4.3e-01
#> 3     no_effect           6.9e-01 4.4e-01

Ignoring direction, flips_sign is the strongest result of the three: it rose sharply in one cohort and fell sharply in another. Give each test its effect (only its sign is used) and mzLib first turns each two-sided p into the one-sided p-value for effect > 0, so opposite effects cancel. The combined p_value is the upper tail: signed, it tests effect > 0, and a Stouffer p_value near 1 means a consistently negative effect.

Before you trust a combined p-value: the studies must be independent (two analyses of the same samples are one study); it is not adjusted across features (send records$p_value to stats_adjust()); and it is not an effect size. If every study reports an estimate and a standard error on one scale, stats_meta() pools those and says how much the studies disagree; prefer it.

Correlating features with a trait

When the samples differ by a number rather than a group - age, dose, the amount loaded - the question is which features rise or fall with it. stats_correlate() answers it with Spearman’s rank correlation: for each feature, mzLib ranks the feature’s values and the trait over the samples where both are known, correlates the ranks, and tests rho = 0, two-sided. It reads stats_fit()’s responses table and a trait table: one row per sample, then one value column, whose header names the trait.

correlation <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                               file.path(data, "malat_dilution_load_ng.tsv"))
correlation
#> <mzlibr_correlations> 492 features x 27 samples against malat_ng
#>   exact 4, asymptotic 308, not_estimable 180
r <- correlation$records
r$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", r$feature)
estimable <- r[r$method != "not_estimable" & r$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc", "20mer2"), ]
aggregate(rho ~ transcript, data = estimable, FUN = median)
#>   transcript       rho
#> 1     20mer2 0.4879500
#> 2       FLuc 0.0000000
#> 3     MALAT1 0.4330127

MALAT1’s oligos rise with its load, and FLuc’s, the spike every run was normalised to, do not.

  • method says how p_value was computed: "exact" (the full permutation distribution, for n of 9 or fewer with no ties, as R’s cor.test()), "asymptotic" (t on n - 2 degrees of freedom, as cor.test(exact = FALSE)), or "not_estimable", where rho and p_value are NA.
  • Small n cannot be significant. Three samples have six orderings, so even a perfect rank correlation on three runs has p = 1/3.
  • An asymptotic p-value of exactly 0 means rho is exactly -1 or 1: the t-test’s limit, not a measured probability.
  • For 10 to 1289 samples without ties, R’s default cor.test() uses an Edgeworth series that mzLib does not, so p-values there differ slightly from R’s default output, but not from cor.test(exact = FALSE). This package’s tests hold every row to cor.test() run in R.

Partial correlation. If something else also varies by sample - batch, run order, sex - give it in a given table of the same shape. mzLib then correlates what is left of the feature’s ranks and the trait’s ranks after each is regressed on the covariates’ ranks, as ppcor::pcor.test(method = "spearman") does:

plain <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "limma_reference_age.tsv"))
partial <- stats_correlate(file.path(data, "limma_reference_responses.tsv"),
                           file.path(data, "limma_reference_age.tsv"),
                           given = file.path(data, "limma_reference_sex.tsv"))
rbind(plain = plain$method_counts, given_sex = partial$method_counts)
#>           exact asymptotic not_estimable
#> plain        22        378             0
#> given_sex     0        400             0
head(data.frame(feature = plain$records$feature, rho = round(plain$records$rho, 2),
                rho_given_sex = round(partial$records$rho, 2)), 5)
#>   feature  rho rho_given_sex
#> 1      g1 0.38          0.37
#> 2      g2 0.93          0.97
#> 3      g3 0.65          0.64
#> 4      g4 0.12          0.12
#> 5      g5 0.43          0.37

The partial test is always asymptotic, on n - 2 - k degrees of freedom for k covariates. Partial out only nuisance variables: a covariate that follows the trait takes the trait’s signal with it.

Is a feature’s detection related to the condition?

Missing values in label-free data are rarely random: a protein near the detection limit is missed more often where there is less of it. Ask the data first: does each feature’s chance of being detected depend on the condition? That is a logistic regression per feature on a table of 1 (measured) and 0 (not measured). stats_fit_logistic() runs one per feature, as R’s glm(family = binomial), and tests each coefficient with a Wald z. The dilution series has a detection table: 1 where the responses file has a value, 0 where it is blank.

detection <- stats_fit_logistic(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_detected.tsv"),
                                file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"),
                                c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
detection$status_counts
#>               fitted too_few_observations       rank_deficient 
#>                  191                    0                    0 
#>            separated        not_converged 
#>                  301                    0
quarter <- detection$records[detection$records$coefficient == "malat_125ng", ]
quarter$transcript <- sub(":.*$", "", quarter$feature)
detected <- quarter[quarter$status == "fitted" & quarter$transcript %in% c("MALAT1", "FLuc"), ]
aggregate(estimate ~ transcript, data = detected, FUN = median)
#>   transcript   estimate
#> 1       FLuc  0.4054651
#> 2     MALAT1 -0.1823216

estimate is a change in the log-odds of detection: for a 0/1 column, the log of the odds ratio against the 500 ng runs.

A separated feature has no estimate, and that is not the same as no effect. When the design splits a feature’s 0s from its 1s, no maximum-likelihood estimate exists. R’s glm() prints a huge coefficient and a warning there; mzLib reports "separated" and NA. Most oligos here are separated because they were seen in a handful of runs, or none:

separated <- quarter[quarter$status == "separated", ]
head(sort(table(events = separated$events), decreasing = TRUE), 4)
#> events
#>  0  2  1  3 
#> 64 55 54 37

Here separation means “too sparse to say”. In a cleaner experiment the same status can mark the strongest result in the table - a protein detected in every treated sample and in no control - so read events and observed before you discard one. Against R’s glm(), on mzLib’s own reference input:

glm_fit <- stats_fit_logistic(file.path(data, "glm_reference_responses.tsv"),
                              file.path(data, "glm_reference_design.tsv"), c("Intercept", "x", "grp"))
glm <- read.delim(file.path(data, "glm_reference_fit.tsv"))
x <- glm_fit$records[glm_fit$records$coefficient == "x", ]
ok <- glm$status == "fitted"
c(estimate = worst(x$estimate[ok], glm$b1[ok]), standard_error = worst(x$standard_error[ok], glm$se1[ok]))
#>       estimate standard_error 
#>   4.203008e-12   1.341800e-07

The estimates agree to better than 1e-8 and the standard errors to 1e-6 (summary.glm() takes its weights from the step before the estimate). Wald tests are weakest near separation and in small samples, and no likelihood-ratio test is offered. A 0 is an outcome: blank only a cell you genuinely do not know.

When samples come in groups

Runs acquired on different days, replicates from one donor, studies pooled into one analysis: each group can sit at its own baseline. stats_fit() treats every sample as independent, so a day-to-day shift either inflates its residual variance or, when the days are unbalanced, leaks into the effect. A mixed model gives every group its own baseline, a random intercept with variance tau^2, and estimates each coefficient within groups: stats_fit_mixed(), as nlme::lme(y ~ ..., random = ~ 1 | group) per feature. The dilution series’ runs were acquired on five days; a groups table says which:

mixed <- stats_fit_mixed(file.path(data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "malat_dilution_design.tsv"),
                         file.path(data, "malat_dilution_day.tsv"), c("malat_250ng", "malat_125ng"))
mixed
#> <mzlibr_mixed_model_fit> 492 features x 27 samples in 5 groups (day), reml, reporting malat_250ng, malat_125ng
#>   fitted 210, too_few_observations 214, rank_deficient 66, too_few_groups 2, variance_ratio_at_limit 0, not_converged 0
malat_medians <- function(result) {
  r <- result$records[result$records$status == "fitted" & startsWith(result$records$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
  aggregate(cbind(estimate, standard_error) ~ coefficient, data = r, FUN = median)
}
malat_medians(fit)
#>   coefficient   estimate standard_error
#> 1 malat_125ng -1.0144266      1.0888865
#> 2 malat_250ng -0.8914901      0.9967881
malat_medians(mixed)
#>   coefficient  estimate standard_error
#> 1 malat_125ng -1.093018      0.6977282
#> 2 malat_250ng -1.048479      0.7064118

The design is unchanged: do not add a column per day, the random intercept replaces it. estimator is "reml" because none was given and that is mzLib’s default. Within days, the median standard errors are smaller: the day-to-day shift no longer counts as noise.

  • A coefficient constant within each group is tested on the groups. Its df is nlme’s “containment” df, a whole number per row; with too few groups there is none, and p_value is NA while t is reported.
  • group_variance 0 is the boundary: no group effect. nlme cannot reach 0 and reports a tiny positive value there instead.
  • Under "reml" the log-likelihood is restricted: compare it only between models with the same fixed effects, and use estimator = "ml" to compare designs.

Against nlme, on mzLib’s own reference input (seven groups of unequal size):

lmm <- stats_fit_mixed(file.path(data, "lmm_reference_responses.tsv"),
                       file.path(data, "lmm_reference_design.tsv"),
                       file.path(data, "lmm_reference_groups.tsv"), c("Intercept", "age", "wp"))
nlme <- read.delim(file.path(data, "lmm_reference_fit.tsv"))
nlme <- nlme[nlme$method == "REML", ]
age <- lmm$records[lmm$records$coefficient == "age", ]
c(estimate = worst(age$estimate, nlme$b1), standard_error = worst(age$standard_error, nlme$se1))
#>       estimate standard_error 
#>   1.610138e-06   2.195060e-07
all(age$df == nlme$df1)
#> [1] TRUE

mzLib matches nlme to 1e-5 relative (nlme’s own optimizer precision). Satterthwaite and Kenward-Roger df (lmerTest) are not implemented, so p-values differ from lmerTest’s.

When some samples are only counted

You want to know Call mzLib computes it with
Does a value follow a trait, when some runs measured it and others only counted successes (k of n)? stats_fit_latent_mixed() LogitNormalMixedModel.Fit (#1469)
How does a count’s chance of success follow the value (the link)? stats_fit_link() LogitNormalMixedModel.FitLink (#1469)

Some quantities are measured in some runs and only counted in others. A PTM site’s occupancy is the usual case: where the modified and unmodified peptides were both quantified, you have a number; where they were not, you may know only that 3 of 8 covering peptidoforms carried the modification. stats_fit_mixed() has to drop the counted runs. stats_fit_latent_mixed() uses both kinds.

It models a latent value per run, such as the log-odds of the site’s occupancy, with stats_fit_mixed()’s structure: fixed effects from your design, a random intercept per group (an animal, a donor), and run-to-run scatter. A measured run reads the latent value. A counted run has k of its n trials succeed, each with a chance g set by the latent value through a link: logit g = intercept + slope x latent + depth_slope x depth. With the identity link (0, 1), a count samples the same probability a measurement reads. The model is a binomial generalized linear mixed model (Breslow and Clayton 1993), the kind R users fit with lme4::glmer (Bates et al. 2015).

You choose which cells are counted, and the link. mzLibR builds neither. mzLib’s PTM-QTL code does not yet do it either, so the counts table is yours to write.

mzLib’s own test of this model simulates 16 animals of 4 runs each, with a trait that is 0 or 1 per animal and a true trait effect of 1.0 on the latent scale. Every other run is measured; the rest are counted, 5 trials each, through the link (0.4, 0.6). The package ships three of those simulations, one per feature. The counts table has the responses table’s layout, each cell successes/trials:

counts <- read.delim(file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_counts.tsv"), colClasses = "character")
counts[1, 1:5]
#>   feature s1  s2 s3  s4
#> 1   seed1    3/5    2/5
latent <- stats_fit_latent_mixed(file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_design.tsv"),
  file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_groups.tsv"), c("Intercept", "trait"), link = c(0.4, 0.6),
  responses = file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_responses.tsv"),
  counts = file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_counts.tsv"))
latent
#> <mzlibr_latent_mixed_model_fit> 3 features x 64 samples in 16 groups (animal), reml, reporting Intercept, trait
#>   96 measured and 96 counted cells, through logit g = 0.4 + 0.6 x latent + 0 x depth, overdispersion 0
#>   fitted 3, too_few_observations 0, rank_deficient 0, separated 0, not_converged 0, too_few_groups 0
unlist(latent$link)
#>      intercept          slope    depth_slope overdispersion 
#>            0.4            0.6            0.0            0.0

link echoes what mzLib used. The depth slope and overdispersion were not given, so they are mzLib’s defaults. Now fit the measured runs alone with stats_fit_mixed(), and compare:

measured <- stats_fit_mixed(file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_responses.tsv"),
  file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_design.tsv"), file.path(data, "lnmm_simulated_groups.tsv"),
  c("Intercept", "trait"))
ours <- latent$records[latent$records$coefficient == "trait", ]
theirs <- measured$records[measured$records$coefficient == "trait", ]
data.frame(feature = ours$feature,
           latent = sprintf("%+.2f +- %.2f", ours$estimate, ours$standard_error),
           runs = paste(ours$measured, "+", ours$counted),
           measured_only = sprintf("%+.2f +- %.2f", theirs$estimate, theirs$standard_error),
           measured_runs = theirs$observed)
#>   feature        latent    runs measured_only measured_runs
#> 1   seed1 +1.61 +- 0.33 32 + 32 +1.63 +- 0.33            32
#> 2   seed2 +0.73 +- 0.26 32 + 32 +0.77 +- 0.27            32
#> 3   seed3 +1.26 +- 0.28 32 + 32 +1.36 +- 0.28            32
rbind(latent = latent$records$df[latent$records$coefficient == "Intercept"],
      measured_only = measured$records$df[measured$records$coefficient == "Intercept"])
#>               [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> latent          48   48   48
#> measured_only   16   16   16

Every trait estimate is within 2 standard errors of the true 1.0 (mzLib’s own test asks for 3):

all(abs(ours$estimate - 1) < 2 * ours$standard_error)
#> [1] TRUE

The counted runs barely shrink the trait’s standard error, and that is correct. The trait is constant within each animal, so it is tested between animals, on 16 animals minus 2 coefficients, 14 df in both fits. More runs per animal sharpen each animal’s baseline, but the number of animals limits how sure you can be about the trait. Effects that vary within animals gain more: the intercept is tested on 48 df with the counts, against 16 without.

What each row says, beyond stats_fit_mixed()’s columns:

  • estimate and standard_error are on the latent scale: natural log-odds here, so exp(estimate) is an odds ratio of occupancy.
  • measured and counted are the runs of each kind the feature contributed. df counts both.
  • residual_variance_given is TRUE when sigma^2 came from your residual_variance table rather than the fit. Give it for a feature with too few measured runs to estimate its scatter.
  • status can be "separated": the counts are split by the design (every run of one group all 0, of another all full), so the estimate runs to infinity. You get the status, never a p-value.

Check it against lme4 and glmmTMB. mzLib’s reference input is 16 simulated features over 23 runs in 8 animals, every run counted, through the link (-0.4, 0.6, 0.3) with a depth term, and R’s glmer fit of each with 25-point adaptive quadrature. Those fits have no run-to-run scatter, so each feature is given mzLib’s tiny sigma^2 of 2e-7, as mzLib’s own comparison does:

counted <- stats_fit_latent_mixed(file.path(data, "lnmm_reference_design.tsv"),
  file.path(data, "lnmm_reference_groups.tsv"), c("Intercept", "trait", "x"),
  link = c(-0.4, 0.6, 0.3), counts = file.path(data, "lnmm_link_counts.tsv"),
  depth = file.path(data, "lnmm_link_depth.tsv"),
  residual_variance = file.path(data, "lnmm_link_residual_variance.tsv"), estimator = "ml")
glmer <- read.delim(file.path(data, "lnmm_counted_fit.tsv"))
glmer <- glmer[glmer$link == "link" & glmer$method == "ML", ]
sapply(c(Intercept = 0, trait = 1, x = 2), function(j) {
  ours <- counted$records[counted$records$coefficient == c("Intercept", "trait", "x")[j + 1], ]
  max(abs(ours$estimate - glmer[[paste0("b", j)]]) / glmer[[paste0("se", j)]]) < 1e-5
})
#> Intercept     trait         x 
#>      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE

Every estimate is within 1e-5 of glmer’s standard error from glmer’s own. With run-to-run scatter estimated from counts alone, the reference is glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017), which integrates by a Laplace approximation where mzLib uses quadrature, so they agree to about 1%:

scatter <- stats_fit_latent_mixed(file.path(data, "lnmm_reference_design.tsv"),
  file.path(data, "lnmm_reference_groups.tsv"), c("Intercept", "trait", "x"), link = "identity",
  counts = file.path(data, "lnmm_scatter_counts.tsv"))
tmb <- read.delim(file.path(data, "lnmm_scatter_fit.tsv"))
tmb <- tmb[tmb$method == "REML", ]
trait <- scatter$records[scatter$records$coefficient == "trait", ]
c(group_variance = max(abs(trait$group_variance - tmb$tau2) / tmb$tau2) < 0.03,
  standard_error = max(abs(trait$standard_error - tmb$se1) / tmb$se1) < 0.03)
#> group_variance standard_error 
#>           TRUE           TRUE

Fitting the link

The identity link says a count samples the very probability a measurement reads. Often it does not: whether a modified form is seen at all depends on how much of it there is, not only on its share. stats_fit_link() fits the link from cells: each with a count and the normal its latent value is taken to sit at (a mean and an SD, such as its feature’s mean and SD over the measured runs, mzLib’s own suggestion). By default it fits on detection: whether any trial succeeded, the event that makes a covered zero.

mzLib’s own test of FitLink simulates 4,000 cells through the link (-0.5, 0.5, 0.3) with a depth term, and the package ships them:

link <- stats_fit_link(file.path(data, "link_cells.tsv"), with_depth = TRUE)
str(link[c("cell_count", "with_depth", "with_overdispersion", "detection_only")])
#> List of 4
#>  $ cell_count         : num 4000
#>  $ with_depth         : logi TRUE
#>  $ with_overdispersion: logi FALSE
#>  $ detection_only     : logi TRUE
round(unlist(link$link), 2)
#>      intercept          slope    depth_slope overdispersion 
#>          -0.51           0.51           0.33           0.00

The link is recovered from detection alone. with_overdispersion and detection_only were left out, so they are mzLib’s defaults, which the result reports. stats_fit_link()’s result goes straight into stats_fit_latent_mixed(link = ).

Before you trust a latent-scale mixed model:

  • The inputs are on the latent scale. Send logit occupancy, not a fraction or an intensity.
  • The link is a modelling choice. The identity link assumes a count samples the latent value itself; a fitted one depends on the cells you chose.
  • Standard errors are at the estimated variances. They do not include those variances’ own uncertainty, so they are not glmmTMB’s vcov().
  • Under "reml", the fixed effects are integrated out by a Laplace approximation, as glmmTMB’s REML = TRUE does. With nothing counted it is exactly stats_fit_mixed()’s REML, and the two agree to about 1e-5. Under "ml", estimates and variances agree with stats_fit_mixed()’s, but its standard errors are scaled differently.
  • The integrals are adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature (Liu and Pierce 1994): 40 nodes over each animal’s baseline, 12 over each count’s run scatter, as glmer’s nAGQ. The source is mzLib/StatisticalModels/LogitNormalMixedModel.cs (mzLib #1469).
  • Not adjusted across features. Send p_value to stats_adjust().

Does a search really control its FDR?

An entrapment experiment adds peptides that cannot be in the sample to the search database. Every entrapment the search reports is then a known false discovery, which lets you check the search’s FDR claim instead of trusting it. stats_entrapment_fdp() computes the three valid estimators of Wen et al. 2025 at each q-value threshold: lower_bound (above your claimed FDR, the search fails to control it; below, it proves nothing), combined (an upper bound: at or below your claimed FDR, evidence of control) and paired (a tighter upper bound for 1:1 pairing). The “sample” estimator N_E / (r N_T) is invalid in both directions and is deliberately absent.

fdp <- stats_entrapment_fdp(file.path(data, "entrapment_reference_targets.tsv"),
                            file.path(data, "entrapment_reference_entrapments.tsv"), ratio = 1)
fdp
#> <mzlibr_entrapment_fdp_estimates> 7 targets, 4 entrapments, ratio 1, 100 of 100 thresholds with a discovery
fdp$records[fdp$records$q_value_threshold %in% c(0.003, 0.01), ]
#>    q_value_threshold target_count entrapment_count lower_bound  combined
#> 3              0.003            2                1   0.3333333 0.6666667
#> 10             0.010            4                3   0.4285714 0.8571429
#>       paired
#> 3  0.3333333
#> 10 0.8571429

This is mzLib’s hand-built search: seven targets and four entrapments. At 1% the search reports 7 discoveries, 3 of them entrapments: far from a 1% FDR. Give one row per unit you estimate for (precursor, peptide or protein group), decoys removed, each with its best q-value; mzLib does not deduplicate. ratio is required: mzLib has no default, and paired is reported only at a ratio of exactly 1, so for 1:1 pairing pass 1, not a ratio computed from database sizes after exclusions.

What to cite

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

  • doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x: the step-up adjustment (Benjamini and Hochberg, J R Stat Soc B 57:289, 1995).
  • doi:10.1111/j.1420-9101.2005.00917.x: the weighted Z (Stouffer) method and why it outperforms Fisher’s for a shared effect (Whitlock, J Evol Biol 18:1368, 2005).
  • doi:10.2307/1412159: the rank correlation coefficient rho (Spearman, Am J Psychol 15:72, 1904).
  • doi:10.5351/CSAM.2015.22.6.665: ppcor, whose pcor.test(method = ‘spearman’) the partial form (–given) reproduces (Kim, Commun Stat Appl Methods 22:665, 2015).
  • doi:10.2307/2347111: the Edgeworth series (AS 89) R’s cor.test uses by default for 10 <= n < 1290, which mzLib does NOT use (Best and Roberts, Appl Stat 24:377, 1975).
  • doi:10.1038/s41592-025-02719-x: the lower-bound (eq. 2), combined (eq. 1) and paired (eq. 4) entrapment estimators mzLib implements, and why the sample estimator is invalid (Wen et al., Nat Methods 22:1454, 2025; the method FDRBench implements).
  • doi:10.1080/01621459.1993.10594284: generalized linear mixed models, the class of model this verb fits: a latent linear predictor with a random intercept, observed through a binomial link (Breslow and Clayton, J Am Stat Assoc 88:9, 1993).
  • doi:10.1093/biomet/81.3.624: adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, centred at the integrand’s mode and scaled by its curvature, which mzLib uses to integrate the counted samples (Liu and Pierce, Biometrika 81:624, 1994).
  • doi:10.18637/jss.v067.i01: lme4’s lmer and glmer (nAGQ 25), the references mzLib’s fits are held to (Bates, Maechler, Bolker and Walker, J Stat Softw 67:1, 2015).
  • doi:10.32614/RJ-2017-066: glmmTMB, whose Laplace-approximated REML mzLib’s REML follows and whose fits with run scatter are a reference (Brooks et al., R Journal 9:378, 2017).
  • doi:10.1093/biomet/58.3.545: restricted maximum likelihood, the default estimator (Patterson and Thompson, Biometrika 58:545, 1971).
  • doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1948.tb00014.x: the beta-binomial distribution, which a link with overdispersion gives a count cell (Skellam, J R Stat Soc B 10:257, 1948).
  • doi:10.1093/comjnl/7.4.308: the simplex search mzLib maximizes the link’s likelihood with (Nelder and Mead, Comput J 7:308, 1965).
  • doi:10.2307/2344614: generalized linear models and their fitting by iteratively reweighted least squares, the estimator mzLib implements (Nelder and Wedderburn, J R Stat Soc A 135:370, 1972).
  • doi:10.1093/biomet/71.1.1: separation: when the outcomes are split by the design the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist, which is the separated status (Albert and Anderson, Biometrika 71:1, 1984).
  • doi:10.2307/2529876: the random-effects linear model y = X beta + Z u + e this verb fits with one random intercept (Laird and Ware, Biometrics 38:963, 1982).
  • doi:10.2202/1544-6115.1027: the empirical-Bayes moderated t this verb computes, for coefficients and contrasts (Smyth, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol 3:3, 2004).
  • doi:10.1093/nar/gkv007: limma, whose eBayes(legacy = TRUE), and contrasts.fit with topTable(confint), mzLib reproduces to 1e-8 relative (Ritchie et al., Nucleic Acids Res 43:e47, 2015).
  • doi:10.1016/0197-2456(86)90046-2: the moment estimator of the between-study variance (DerSimonian and Laird, Control Clin Trials 7:177, 1986).
  • doi:10.18637/jss.v036.i03: metafor, whose rma(method = ‘DL’) mzLib reproduces to 1e-8 relative (Viechtbauer, J Stat Softw 36(3), 2010).
